title: Ancient life in the loaf
text: A sourdough starter is not an ingredient but a {{1}}: flour and water left to catch wild yeasts and bacteria, fed daily, and capable of outliving its baker. Bakers {{2}} starters for decades; some bakeries work with {{3}} more than a century old, and amateur historians have revived starters from dried specimens kept in museum {{4}}. The partnership inside the jar explains the bread. Yeasts raise the dough, releasing carbon dioxide; the bacteria {{5}} the flavour, producing the lactic and acetic acids that give sourdough its taste and its keeping quality. The pair {{6}} each other: the bacteria's acids discourage mould, and the yeast tolerates conditions that would {{7}} faster breads. During the 2020 lockdowns, sourdough became a {{8}} — flour vanished from shops as millions of housebound cooks began feeding jars of their own. Most of those starters are long dead. The culture, however, is fine: every loaf made the old way is a working museum of domesticated wild life, and anyone can start one tonight with two ingredients and patience.

gaps.explanation: 'not an ingredient but a colony' — a living community of microbes; colonel = an army rank, pronounced the same.
'bakers keep starters for decades' — maintain them; the sentence describes a general habit, so the present tense is needed.
'work with cultures more than a century old' — laboratory term for living microbes; currants = dried fruit.
'specimens kept in museum archives' — official stored collections; arsenal = a store of weapons.
'the bacteria furnish the flavour' — supply it; burnish = polish, garnish = decorate a dish.
'the pair protect each other' — shield one another; protrude = stick out.
'conditions that would discourage faster breads' — put them off developing; disparage = belittle.
'sourdough became a craze' — a sudden enthusiastic fashion; crease = a folded line.
